AI model distillation makes yesterday’s intelligence cheap. Frontier labs are worth the rent on tomorrow’s gap — and the option that the frontier begins moving itself.
Three questions decide the economics:
How much intelligence can be distilled?
If everyone distills, who keeps paying to move the frontier?
What is a frontier lab worth in that equilibrium?
Distillation trains a cheaper model on selected frontier-model responses, teaching it to mimic much of the stronger model’s behavior.
Kimi K3, a Chinese open-weight model, has been accused of being distilled from Anthropic’s Fable 5. Whether or not that allegation holds, Kimi matters less for its precise lineage or benchmark rank than for the speed of its arrival: a challenger need only absorb enough frontier behavior to make yesterday’s premium evaporate.
That does not make frontier labs worthless. It identifies the asset. Today’s checkpoint — the saved model — is not the durable value. The value is the lab’s ability to reopen the gap between itself and the best intelligence available cheaply, then collect the excess profit while that gap lasts. Call that frontier rent.

1. How Much Intelligence Can Be Distilled?
A simple example shows why “90% as good” can be misleading
A strong student can reproduce roughly 90% of a frontier model’s ordinary usefulness, but only about 50% of its newest advance — and materially less of its performance on unfamiliar, many-step work.
Suppose the best cheap model is at 80 on an imaginary capability scale. A new frontier model reaches 100. Distillation lifts the cheap model to 90.
To the user, the student looks 90% as capable as the teacher. But it has absorbed only half of the new advance:
(90 − 80) / (100 − 80) = 50%
That is how a model can become an excellent substitute for ordinary use without reproducing the breakthrough that created the new frontier.
Why Discovery Costs More Than Imitation
Pretraining — the vast first stage in which a model learns from text, code, images, and other data — builds the substrate: language, facts, abstractions, and latent problem-solving ability. Reinforcement learning is one of the later stages: the model is rewarded for better answers and gradually learns how to decompose a problem, persist, verify, backtrack, and use tools.
Discovery is expensive. Teaching the discovered behavior can be cheap.
The teacher may explore many failed paths before learning what works. The student is shown the successful paths and skips much of the search. It is the familiar difference between discovering a theorem and teaching it — now automated and sold by the token.
One study made the asymmetry unusually clear. Researchers trained a 32-billion-parameter model on 1,000 carefully selected worked solutions produced by a stronger model. With a simple method for extending its reasoning, the student beat a leading closed reasoning model on two competition-math benchmarks.
A separate experiment reached the same conclusion from the other direction: an also 32-billion-parameter student trained on a frontier teacher’s answers beat a same-sized model given more than 10,000 steps of reinforcement learning.
For a closed teacher, this can still mean tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of paid calls. That is a bill, not a frontier-training budget. Once a capable base model exists, selected teacher outputs can carry a remarkable amount of learned behavior.
Where the Copy Breaks
Distillation works best when the student is already strong, the target task appears in the training set, and answers can be checked cheaply. It is also easier when the teacher exposes rich reasoning traces; an application interface that returns only final answers leaks less. Mathematics, coding, extraction, and structured tool use are ideal. Obscure knowledge, genuinely novel problems, and long autonomous workflows are much harder.
The hard tail — the least routine and hardest-to-verify work — is especially resistant. Small differences in judgment and reliability quickly compound across a long chain of actions. A cheap model may draft the memo. It may still fail when asked to run the process that produces the final product.
Distillation commoditizes a discovered method faster than it reproduces the capacity to discover the next one.
2. If Everyone Distills, Who Pays for the Frontier?
The apparent problem is free-riding: why spend billions creating a capability that others can copy?
Because followers copy a frontier that has already been reached.
A lab does not need permanent ownership of one checkpoint. It needs to keep reopening a valuable gap between itself and the best cheap substitute. Three mechanisms make that worth funding.
The Hard Tail Pays
Cheap models will process most tokens. Frontier models can still dominate the smaller class of tasks for which failure is expensive.
The value of artificial intelligence is not proportional to token volume. Summarizing another meeting may be worth pennies. Reliably completing a software migration, identifying a drug target, redesigning a company’s workflow, or finding the flaw in a bond covenant can be worth thousands or millions.
The likely market will route routine work to cheap models and escalate difficult or uncertain work to the frontier. Distillation creates the mass market. The frontier becomes the completion layer.
The Leader Distills Itself
The frontier lab owns the best teacher first.
It can use that teacher to build cheaper models for coding, devices, consumer use, and specialized industries. Easy work runs on its students; difficult work escalates to its frontier model. One research program supports an entire product ladder.
The same process that helps competitors copy yesterday’s model therefore helps the leader monetize today’s model at every price point.
A Temporary Lead Can Become a Durable Position
Even a short model lead can outlive the checkpoint.
During that window, a lab can win enterprise deployments, integrate into workflows, attract developers, collect proprietary usage data, and establish its software for multi-step work as the default. The technical gap fades; the installed system may remain.
That is why frontier training will be funded not only by standalone labs, but by cloud platforms that sell computing power, software companies defending their customer base, chip companies feeding the buildout, and states treating advanced intelligence as strategic infrastructure.
Frontier training does not require a permanent monopoly. First use, self-distillation, distribution, complementary businesses, and strategic necessity are enough.
3. What Is a Frontier Lab Worth?
The market keeps trying to value frontier labs as unusually fast-growing software companies. That prices the wrong asset.
The economically relevant quantity is frontier rent:
The profit earned because a lab is ahead of the best cheap alternative, after paying the cost of running its models and doing the research required to remain ahead.
A checkpoint has little terminal value. A repeatable capacity to generate frontier rent can have enormous terminal value. A lab that cannot renew the lead loses the rent quickly; one great model is a windfall, not a franchise.
The clean valuation is:
Lab value = capitalized frontier rent + durable platform value + the option on recursive self-improvement.
The terms should not be double-counted. Frontier rent is the excess profit created by a capability lead. Platform value is what survives after that lead narrows: distribution, customer workflows, proprietary context, and switching costs.
Price the Rent
Capitalizing frontier rent at 18–20 times, a $900 billion operating value requires roughly $45–50 billion of sustainable annual rent.
That is demanding, not fantastical, when compared with the global market for skilled labor rather than today’s chatbot subscriptions. Fifty million professional users or agents — models given tools and multi-step jobs — yielding $1,000 each in annual rent gets there.
The key word is rent, not value created. Customers may receive far more than $1,000 of benefit. The lab must retain enough pricing power to charge for the difference between its model and the cheap substitute.
My base case is that a genuine top-tier lab could sustain $40–60 billion of annual frontier rent near the end of the decade. At roughly 18 times, that supports $700 billion to $1.1 trillion at maturity. Because the rent arrives in the future and requires more capital to reach, it does not by itself justify a $900 billion value today. The rest must come from a platform that survives model parity and from the option on a much larger outcome.
The market may therefore be roughly right about the value of occupying the frontier while being wildly optimistic about how many firms can live there.
Price the Platform
Platform value is what remains after another model becomes just as capable: distribution, embedded workflows, proprietary customer context, developer tools, and switching costs. It belongs in the valuation only if customers stay when the technical lead disappears.
Otherwise, calling the same advantage first “frontier rent” and then “platform value” is not valuation. It is enthusiasm with a spreadsheet.
Price the Option
A leading frontier lab also owns a call option on recursive self-improvement: a model becoming materially better at the research and engineering required to build its successor.
That option is no longer conference-panel theology. In 2026, a general-purpose frontier model that had not been trained specifically for cybersecurity began finding and exploiting previously unknown vulnerabilities across major operating systems and browsers. Mozilla shipped fixes for 271 Firefox vulnerabilities found during one model-assisted program. In a narrow cyber benchmark, independent evaluators estimated that the length of tasks models could complete autonomously had been doubling about every 4.7 months before the newest models jumped ahead of that trend.
Cybersecurity is not recursive self-improvement. It is evidence that a general model can abruptly acquire a rare expert research capability as a side effect of broader gains.
If that transfer reaches artificial-intelligence research — experiment design, data curation, systems optimization, architecture search — the loop begins to close. Hardware, energy, and experiment time still constrain it, but they do not make it a small option.
The payoff is highly convex. The same uncertainty cuts two ways: it lowers the value of ordinary cash flows, but raises the value of the option. If the loop never closes, the option expires. If one lab closes it first and retains the lead, the option may become almost the entire company.
The option is valuable only to the extent that it is early and exclusive. A simultaneous breakthrough is a scientific event, not a monopoly.
A discounted-cash-flow model can price the rent. Around a self-accelerating intelligence loop, it becomes rather bashful.
Conclusion
Distillation will erase much of the premium on ordinary intelligence, but not necessarily the value of discovering the next capability.
Frontier training survives because a temporary lead can pay through the hard tail, self-distillation, distribution, and strategic demand.
A frontier lab is therefore worth the rent it can repeatedly recreate, the platform value that survives model parity, and the option that the research process begins to accelerate.
The model will be copied. The lab earns its value by moving first again.And if the frontier begins moving itself, the option becomes the company.
